newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Moscow honours Greek saviour of modern Russian art.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Moscow honours Greek saviour of modern Russian art.

text.p: To most of his contemporaries George Costakis was "a mad Greek buying hideous paintings".

Even his friends were puzzled by his unfashionable penchant for abstract art, but today Costakis is revered by Russia's art world as the man who single-handedly saved thousands of avant-garde works from oblivion.
Seven years after Costakis' death in Greece, Moscow is honouring his memory with the biggest exhibition to date of paintings and drawings from his unique collection.
"I think we would have lost many great works of art without Costakis," said Jan Brook, deputy director of research at the Tretyakov Gallery which is staging the exhibition.
The Moscow News weekly went further. "Without Costakis there would be no Russian avant-garde," it said.

The exhibition, comprising around 200 of the main works which Costakis bequeathed to the Tretyakov when he left Russia in 1977, includes paintings and drawings by Marc Chagall, Kazimir Malevich, Vasily Kandinsky and Vladimir Tatlin.
"Costakis did not collect just for his own private enjoyment, he wanted to create something of lasting, historical value and he succeeded," Brook told Reuters.
REVOLUTION TURNS FULL CIRCLE

Such praise would have been unthinkable in communist times when Kostakis, born in Moscow in 1913 to a Greek mercantile family, was scouring the Soviet capital for the non-figurative, geometric and constructivist works that Russia had rejected.
"The earth will become sky and the sky will become earth before the Russians acknowledge this art," Costakis would later recall art experts as telling him.
In Russia, as elsewhere, the first three decades of the 20th century were a period of radical experimentation in the arts.

Futurists published manifestoes entitled "Go to the Devil" and "A Slap to Public Taste" and declared in 1917, the year of the Bolshevik revolution, that Art had been abolished along with the old Tsarist regime.
"It is time for art to invade life," they proclaimed, seeing in the revolution a chance to discard all conventions and institutions, including galleries and academies.

But the euphoria was short-lived. As the Bolsheviks tightened their grip on power under Josef Stalin the avant-garde's bold iconoclasm fell into disfavour and Socialist Realism, which lauded Russia's workers and peasants, held sway.
COSTAKIS THE DETECTIVE
Costakis, who never formally studied art, first acquired a taste for paintings while working as a chauffeur for the Greek embassy and later for the Canadian embassy.

"He became a kind of detective. Friends and relatives of the painters he admired would start contacting him, offering him works when they realised he was a serious collector," said Maria Tsautsanoglou of the Greek Embassy in Moscow.

He found paintings under beds, in attics, on snow-covered balconies. His search was often frustrated by the fear of most Russians in the Cold War period of contact with foreigners, but he had an uncanny eye for masterpieces.
His friend, British writer Bruce Chatwin, described how Costakis blew the money he had saved up to buy a car on a Chagall painting, much to his wife's annoyance.

Gradually, Costakis' apartment in a bleak Moscow suburb became a place of pilgrimage for Russian and foreign art lovers. Diplomats, dissidents, scholars and the merely curious would meet there to admire his collection and talk about art.

Photographs from that time show the walls of his apartment ablaze with vibrant colours and elemental forms, Chagall dreamscapes and Malevich's monochrome receneration of Russian artists discovered their own country's avant-garde heritage right there in Costakis' flat," said Tsautsanoglou.
Costakis' dream was to have his collection housed in a new Soviet museum dedicated to contemporary art bearing his name, she said.
MONEY PROBLEMS OVERSHADOW EXHIBITION

This dream was never realised but he decided to donate the bulk of his paintings to the Tretyakov when he moved to Athens. He also had the satisfaction, shortly before his death, of finally seeing a small part of his collection on public display in Moscow.
Though Costakis' reputation is secure in Russia today the current exhibition has not been entirely trouble-free.
Plans to display the whole collection fell victim to Russia's economic woes and the pictures he took to Greece are missing from the exhibition, Brook said.
The Moscow exhibition had originally been intended as the last leg in a tour that took the collection from Athens to Germany, France and Finland.
But the Tretyakov, strapped for cash like most Russian cultural institutions, has not even been able to publish a catalogue.

And the exhibition comes at a sensitive time for the Russian art world as Germany steps up pressure on Moscow to return works plundered from German museums and private collections by the Soviet Red Army during and after World War Two.

Writing in Moscow News, journalist Andrei Tolstoy said the long saga of Costakis' collection should give Russians -- usually fiercely proud of their country's cultural accomplishments -- pause for reflection.

"Today we do not want to give up art treasures taken by us after the war but we forget that until now we have been unable to preserve even our own national art," he said, referring to the decades-long neglect of the avant-garde.
"And it is a pity that we have not been able, even now, to bring together the Moscow and the Greek parts of a once single collection."
